sentences.text: Taniwhasaurus is an extinct genus of marine lizards known as mosasaurs that lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
It was a medium-sized mosasaur with a maximum estimated length of around 6.7 meters, making it shorter than its relative Tylosaurus.
The skull of Taniwhasaurus is triangular in shape when viewed from above.
Dental counts differ between species, with T. oweni having 14 maxillary teeth while T. antarcticus has 12.
The neural spine of the axis vertebra is stout and elongated, ending in a broad, flattened spike that likely supported a cartilaginous cap.
The tail vertebrae of Taniwhasaurus had a subcircular shape in the front that became ovoid and laterally compressed towards the back.
CT scans of T. antarcticus suggest that Taniwhasaurus likely possessed an electro-sensitive organ capable of detecting prey movements underwater, similar to modern aquatic predators.
T. oweni is estimated to have been at least 6 meters long based on the fossil remains.
The genus Taniwhasaurus was first described by the Scottish naturalist James Hector in 1874 based on fossils found in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff, New Zealand.
The type species T. oweni was discovered in the 1860s in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff in eastern New Zealand.

Juan M. Lirio discovered a well-preserved mosasaur specimen in January 2000 on James Ross Island in Antarctica, where the geological formation dates from the late Campanian to late Maastrichtian stages of the Upper Cretaceous.
Fossils of Taniwhasaurus were first collected in the Pondoland region of South Africa at the beginning of the 20th century.
A specimen was found in a floating concretion within the Kashima Formation of the Yezo Group in Hokkaido, dated to the Santonian-Campanian stage.
The short, wide, and muscular humerus with paddle-shaped bones suggests Taniwhasaurus was an efficient swimmer.
Researchers accept that the tail was the main source of propulsion for T. antarcticus, placing its swimming style between eel-like and carangiform forms.
T. antarcticus likely had a high capacity for lateral neck movement, but the muscles involved lacked significant strength.
Researchers hypothesize that the large snout foramina in Taniwhasaurus are correlated with its toothless snout, though this requires further validation.
Two species are currently recognized within the genus: T. antarcticus described by Novas et al. in 2002 and T. mikasaensis described by Caldwell et al. in 2008.
In 1888, Lydekker reclassified Taniwhasaurus as a junior synonym of the genus Platecarpus.
In 1971, Welles and Gregg placed Taniwhasaurus in the subfamily Tylosaurinae based on cranial similarities to Tylosaurus.
Taniwhasaurus was a close relative of the genera Tylosaurus and Hainosaurus and belongs to the parent group Tylosaurinae.

In 2016, Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro proposed reclassifying T. capensis into the genus Taniwhasaurus based on skull characteristics, but in 2019 she and Caldwell noted the fossils were too poorly preserved for a definitive genus-level identification.
In 2019, Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell classified the specimen as an indeterminate species of Taniwhasaurus due to insufficient fossil material for a distinct species diagnosis.
Taniwhasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Campanian stage, with potential records from the Santonian stage in South Africa, Japan, and Russia.
Most species of Taniwhasaurus were endemic to the Weddellian Province of Gondwana, which included Antarctica, New Zealand, and Patagonia.
T. oweni fossils are found in the Conway Formation at Haumuri Bluff, dating to the Lower and Middle Campanian.
Researchers concluded that Tylosaurus haumuriensis is a junior synonym of T. oweni because the differences between the two taxa are mainly due to size rather than distinct morphology.
Subsequent studies have expressed skepticism regarding the claim that a juvenile skull found in the Maastrichtian belongs to T. antarcticus.
In 2019, Jiménez-Huidobro and Caldwell debated whether Taniwhasaurus is monophyletic, noting that some species have fossils too fragmentary for concrete assignment.
